proof: Emulators recreate a console so they can run its library. Retro Porting Toolkit takes a different route: it recompiles one game at a time, preserving the original game logic while replacing the hardware constraints around it. That trades broad compatibility for deeper control over rendering, input, networking, and behavior, and it builds directly on decades of knowledge from the emulation community.

Getting a game to boot correctly is the floor, not the finish line. On its own, a correct recomp mostly buys faster loading. The point is what comes next: performance headroom and extensibility the original hardware could never offer.
philosophy: Go native. Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, even the browser. No emulator core in sight.
See more of the world. Adaptive widescreen up to 21:9 in games like Tomba! 2 and Mega Man Zero.
Break the old limits. 60 FPS patches, CD-quality MSU-1 soundtracks, voxel 3D remixes, and mod loaders that never touch your original ROM.
Swap the hardware. Spin WarioWare: Twisted! with your phone or a DualSense, and let real local weather drive Boktai's solar sensor.
Change the words. Runtime text replacement powers Tsumu Light's English fan translation and NES text overrides.
Play together. Shared netplay, rollback, save states, and rewind (recomp-net and retcomm-rbengine) that every ecosystem can pick up.
constraintsIntro: The team's rule of thumb: the games are the byproduct, the ecosystem is the product. And every enhancement follows one hard rule: the original game file is never modified. Features layer over a verified, untouched copy at runtime, and turning them off returns the authentic game, byte for byte.

stories.title: The screen was the limit. Not anymore.
stories.body: Many GBA games keep whole maps in memory; the screen was the only thing hiding them. Adaptive widescreen widens the real view up to 21:9: The Minish Cap shows more of the world, and Mega Man Zero finally gives you room to react.
stories.alt: The Minish Cap running in adaptive 21:9 widescreen

stories.title: One mod loader. Four consoles. Zero patched ROMs.
stories.body: PlayStation, SNES, GBA, and Genesis now share an opt-in mod loader. Mega Man X6 ships an authorized adaptation of the Mega Man X6 Tweaks patch, and Tomba! re-enables a debug menu the developers left in the game, no disc patching involved.
stories.alt: The mod list in Mega Man X6 Recompiled

stories.title: Cartridges become modern sensors.
stories.body: WarioWare: Twisted! reads its twist from a controller gyroscope on PC, or from your phone in the Android build. Boktai's solar sensor is on the same path through a community contribution.
stories.alt: WarioWare: Twisted! taking gyro input from a controller and a phone

platformNote.title: One improvement can help many games.
platformNote.body: Capabilities live in shared platform runtimes, so work done for one game carries to the next. The mod loader that proved out on Mega Man X6 now serves four consoles, and the same approach is reaching new frontiers: the original Xbox rendered its first recompiled frame, the GameCube boot menu runs in full, and the CD-i BIOS boots into Hotel Mario.
